newsitem.title: USA: Lobbyist defense rests, case goes to jury Friday.
newsitem.headline: Lobbyist defense rests, case goes to jury Friday.

text.p: Lawyers for lobbyist Jack Williams rested their case without calling any witnesses Thursday to underscore their argument that he did not mislead an investigation into former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy.
Attorney Barry Levine announced, "The defence rests," seconds after lead prosecutor Robert Ray formally ended the government's presentation of evidence in U.S. district court.
Closing arguments were set for Friday in the jury trial.
Williams faced two criminal counts of making false statements when asked about an Espy trip and a scholarship to his girlfriend.
"They didn't prove their case," Levine told reporters. "They (investigators) had this plan of what was important to know, and failed to ask them. They are blaming their failure on him (Williams)."

Williams was the Washington lobbyist for Tyson Foods Inc., a leading U.S. meatpacker, when Espy attended a pro football game in Dallas Jan. 16, 1994, as a Tyson Foods guest and during the time when Espy's girlfriend, Patricia Dempsey, was awarded a $1,200 scholarship by the Tyson Foundation.

Investigators for the Agriculture Department and the FBI said Williams told them he knew nothing about the trip other than what he read in the newspapers and did not even know Dempsey's telephone number.
Other witnesses said Williams paid for Dempsey's airplane ticket for the trip and told Tyson headquarters when she would arrive in Dallas.
With the jury out of the courtroom, Levine asked U.S. District Judge James Robertson to acquit Williams. Robertson deferred ruling on the request.
Legal experts have said the outcome of the Williams trial may be key to the ongoing investigation of Espy by independent counsel Donald Smaltz.

So far the investigation has resulted in more than a dozen indictments against individuals and concerns, but it suffered a setback with the dismissal earlier this month of a related case against Espy's brother, Henry, who was accused of conspiring to accept illegal campaign contributions.
A spokesman for Smaltz said the verdict in the Williams trial would have no bearing on the investigation of Mike Espy.
